Definition

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation involves the delivery of oxygen into the lungs via positive pressure through a face mask without the need for endotracheal intubation.

Non-invasive means using face masks and invasive means ETT tube insertion or surgical airway.

James Heilman, MD, via Wikimedia Commons

CPAP & BPAP

NIPPV is delivered via a full-face mask using either continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BPAP) using a ventilator or stand-alone reusable device.

CPAP provides the same amount of pressure support during inspiration and expiration (5 to 20 mmHg)

PruebasBMA, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons · James Heilman, MD, via Wikimedia Commons

BPAP provides different values for inspiration and expiration (IPAP and EPAP) so it allows for increasing inspiratory pressures up to 15 mm Hg without overwhelming the patient with expiratory resistance, which may remain at 5 to 10 mm Hg.

There are no studies showing a significant advantage to one system over another.

Normal physiology of respiration

Breathing is negative pressure process, negative pressure comes from expansion of the chest (increase in volume) due to elevation of the ribs and relaxation of diaphragm (negative pressure ventilation)

In expiration ribs depresses and diaphragm contract to get the air out leading to positive pressure

Henry Vandyke Carter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

NPPV

NPPV works by increasing the outside pressure, air enters the lungs easier

In COPD, there is air trapping inside the lungs due to emphysema and bronchitis, leading to increased pressures inside them, so by increasing the outside pressures, breathing will be easier

Same applies when the alveoli are filled with water in pulmonary edema

Henry Vandyke Carter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Indications

NPPV is indicated in respiratory failure (hypoxia and/or hypercapnia), that is when the lungs are not working well and they need help

According to American thoracic society and European respiratory journal guidelines, NPPV is strongly recommended in the setting of respiratory failure due to:

Acute exacerbation of COPD where PH < 7.35

Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

NPPV is also effective but to lesser degree in:

Post operative acute respiratory failure

Early NPPV Immunocompromised patients with ARF

Palliation to dyspneic patients in terminal cancer and other terminal conditions

Chest trauma patients with ARF

Chronic stable COPD with hypercapnia

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

Obstructive sleep apnea

Respiratory failure due to neuromuscular disease and restrictive thoracic disorders

NPPV also used for pre oxygenation prior to intubation in any medical condition, or as an alternative to invasive airway management in some cases, such as in patients with DNR or DNI status.

NPPV is not that effective for pneumonia, it may even delay mechanical ventilation leading to worse outcome; it is used only in case of shortages of invasive ventilation equipment and facilities (e.g.during covid 19)

Device setting

CPAP: one pressure setting, start with 5 mmHg and titrate up according to response (clinical improvement and vitals) (max is 20 mmHg)

BPAP: two pressure settings, IPAP start with 10 and EPAP start with 5, the sum of both should be less than 20

Pressures above 20 mmHg for both would lead to abdominal distension

Device parts

Mask: on several types including nose masks, nose-mouth masks and helmets

  • Tubing
  • Oxygen supply
  • Power supply
  • Humidifier
Zboralski, via Wikimedia Commons · Michael Symonds, via Wikimedia Commons

Complications

Mask discomfort

Skin rash secondary to infection or hypersensitivity reactions

nasal bridge ulcers (rare)

Aerophagia and hypersalivation

Ear and sinus pain and gastric insufflation due to the pressure

Serious side effects include pneumothorax, pneumocephalus, pneumomediastinum and aspiration

In patient with heart failure, who are hypotensive, NPPV might aggravate hypotension due to increased intrathoracic pressure, increased right ventricular afterload and decreased preload

Patient ventilator dyssynchrony in BPAP: failure to trigger the breathing cycle leading to IPAP applied during expiration and EPAP applied during inspiration which lead to inadequate gas exchange and unnecessary expiratory muscle use , e.g. in COPD where rapid inhalations may not give the BPAP adequate time to cycle from inspiration to expiration thus patient is expiring against ventilator effort to deliver inspiratory pressure leading to respiratory distress

Also failure to trigger can be seen in Neuromuscular disease such as ALS where patient cannot generate enough negative pressure during inspiration to trigger assisted breath

Contraindications

Patient with a lot of secretions requiring frequent suckers

Vomiting

Agitation

Comatose patient

Sedated patient

Hypotensive patient

Prognosis

NPPV has been shown to reduce intubation in COPD and cardiogenic pulmonary edema

It is also shown to reduce the need for reintubation in hypercapnic respiratory failure following extubation.
